newsitem.title: POLAND: WALESA TELLS POLISH AUTHORITIES: SEE YOU IN COURT.
newsitem.headline: WALESA TELLS POLISH AUTHORITIES: SEE YOU IN COURT.

text.p: Lech Walesa defied Poland's ex-communist authorities on Wednesday to take him to court on charges that he had failed to return secret state documents after ceasing to be president in December.
Warsaw prosecutors announced on Tuesday that the UOP security service had laid a complaint against Walesa, alleging a crime which could carry a three-year jail term.

Walesa told Gazeta Wyborcza daily he had accounted for all secret documents at the end of his five-year term as president and the move was an attack on him by his foes now in power, who had already pursued him unfairly for back taxes.
"My tax affair is winding up, so they had to find something else," Walesa told the top-selling daily.
Walesa said he would happily stand before the State Tribunal, a special court for top officials, saying this would only help the opposition in parliamentary elections next year.
"Just stand me before the Tribunal. This would be an ideal election campaign," said the former shipyard electrician who led the Solidarity union to its triumph over communism in 1989.
Neither the UOP State Security Bureau nor the prosecutors would reveal which missing documents, from UOP and the interior ministry, were involved in the proceedings.

Some media reports, including that of the pro-government newspaper Trybuna, suggested the issue may concern some of Walesa's own security police files from the 1970s and 1980s, which he earlier said he had managed to buy.
But Walesa denied to Gazeta that he actually had them.

The move against Walesa coincided with the government's publication of secret documents from a probe of allegations last year that the then prime minister, ex-communist Jozef Oleksy had informed for Moscow spies.

The spy allegations were announced to parliament in December by a minister allied to Walesa, just as he was about to hand over the presidency to ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski who had beaten him in presidential elections.
Oleksy denied any wrongdoing but quit in January this year.
Prosecutors later ruled the evidence against Oleksy was so weak that they dropped the investigation, but public opinion remains sharply divided over the issue.

Walesa and his allies suggested the authorities, dominated by Oleksy's ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party, may have instigated accusations against Walesa in a communist-era style stunt to divert attention away from Oleksy and onto him.

"This gives the impression of an orchestrated action in which special services employees, as in the old days, become a tool in the hands of the ruling politicians," Gazeta Wyborcza's editor Adam Michnik wrote in an editorial.
UOP officials said that they had approached Walesa in writing for the return of the allegedly missing documents and had only taken legal action after he failed to reply.
Walesa, who was due to visit Taiwan this week, has been trying to unite opposition groups, including Solidarity, to beat the ex-communists in parliamentary polls next year.
He has said he does not intend to run for election himself.
